newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's Daiei slips into the red on poor sales.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Daiei slips into the red on poor sales.

text.p: Japan's largest retail chain operator, Daiei Inc, slipped into the red last business year, as a food poisoning epidemic and unseasonal weather depressed sales.

Announcing its annual results on Friday, Daiei said it suffered a group net loss of 11.9 billion yen ($94.4 million) in the year to February 1997 after a net profit of 5.08 billion yen ($40.3 million) in 1995/96.
Daiei's sales of fresh foodstuffs were hurt by a food-poisoning epidemic, which, combined with an unusually cool summer, also caused disappointing sales of clothing and outdoor goods.
Group sales at the company, which operates a nationwide network of supermarkets, slipped 0.3 percent to 3.15 trillion yen ($25 billion) in 1996/97.

Daiei's parent current profit nosedived, falling 98 percent to 591 million yen ($4.69 million) from the previous year's 25.04 billion yen ($198 million). Current profit is pre-tax and includes losses or gains on investments such as shareholdings in other firms. Parent sales were down 0.1 percent to 2.51 trillion yen ($19.9 billion) in 1996/97. Current profit is pre-tax and includes gains and losses made on investments.
"Our business was especially affected by the O-157 food poisoning epidemic as well as sluggish sales of seasonal marchandise," Daiei executive vice president Jun Nakauchi told a news conference.

Analysts said Daiei's reputation had also suffered as a result of staff cuts and a shift to self-service shopping in the last several years. The move alienated some customers who value personal service.

Analysts said Daiei was only able to stay out of the red on a parent basis because it sold 14 billion yen ($111 million) worth of shares it held in major Japanese department store Takashimaya Co Ltd to another Japanese department store, Printemps Ginza SA, in August.
Daiei predicted it would return to profit on a group basis in the 1997/98 year, with a net profit of five billion yen ($39.6 million), but analysts said the road ahead looked bumpy.
Some even said it would take several years for the retailer to rebuild its image.
For 1997/98, Daiei predicted parent sales of 2.6 trillion yen ($20.6 billion) and a parent current profit of 10 billion yen ($79.3 million). ($1=126)
